questions.question: When should you use cookies, localStorage, or sessionStorage?
questions.title: Choosing browser storage
questions.direct_answer: Use cookies when small data must accompany matching HTTP requests, localStorage for small non-sensitive same-origin state that should persist, and sessionStorage for small non-sensitive state isolated to one tab session. The choice depends on transport, lifetime, scope, security, and size.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to choose storage from data ownership and lifecycle rather than convenience.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting every token in localStorage or storing large application records in cookies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: All client storage can be cleared or restricted and should not be the only authoritative copy of important data.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Cookies can travel automatically with matching HTTP requests.
localStorage persists and is shared by same-origin tabs.
sessionStorage is isolated by origin and top-level tab.
None is a safe home for large, secret, or authoritative records.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Cookies, localStorage, and sessionStorage solve different state problems. A cookie can be included automatically with matching HTTP requests, while Web Storage is read by same-origin JavaScript and is not attached to requests.

localStorage is for small non-sensitive state that should survive visits and be visible to same-origin tabs. sessionStorage is for similar state that should stay inside one top-level tab's page session.

For example, an opaque login session ID is commonly carried in a short-lived `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite` cookie so browser JavaScript cannot read it. A selected theme can use localStorage, and an unfinished one-tab checkout step can use sessionStorage.

Cookies add request overhead and need CSRF protection when used for authentication. Web Storage is synchronous and readable by any script running in the origin, so an XSS flaw can expose its values.

The final choice follows data flow: use a cookie only when the server needs the value on requests, choose Web Storage by lifetime and tab scope, and use IndexedDB or the server for larger or authoritative data.

sections.title: Ask where the value must travel
sections.content: Transport is the first dividing line. A server cannot receive Web Storage automatically; application code must read it and deliberately send something. A cookie can be attached by the browser even when JavaScript cannot read it. Lifetime and tab scope then separate the two Web Storage choices.

sections.title: Authentication changes the threat model
sections.content: An HttpOnly session cookie reduces direct token theft through injected JavaScript, but the browser still sends it on eligible requests, so CSRF and XSS effects remain relevant. A bearer token in localStorage avoids automatic cookie attachment but is directly readable by same-origin script. Security depends on the full architecture, expiry, rotation, CSP, CSRF controls, and backend validation—not a storage slogan.

sections.title: Storage decision map
sections.content:
| Need | Typical fit | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Send small value with HTTP requests | Cookie | Scope, overhead, CSRF, expiry |
| Remember small preference across visits | localStorage | Script-readable and synchronous |
| Keep a draft within one tab | sessionStorage | Cleared with the page session |
| Store larger structured/queryable data | IndexedDB | More complex asynchronous API |
| Store authoritative business data | Server/database | Requires network and access control |

questions.question: How should you store and read JSON safely with Web Storage?
questions.title: Safe JSON in Web Storage
questions.direct_answer: Serialize a small value with JSON.stringify(), parse it inside error handling, and validate the resulting shape before use. Reads can return null or old data, and writes can fail because storage is blocked, unavailable, or full.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of serialization, versioning, validation, and storage failures.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming JSON.parse() proves the data has the expected fields or that setItem() always succeeds.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Web Storage is synchronous and string-only; large or frequently updated datasets belong in an asynchronous store such as IndexedDB.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Web Storage values are strings, so objects need JSON serialization.
Missing or malformed values require a safe fallback.
Parsed data must still be checked for the expected shape and version.
setItem() can throw, and client storage can disappear at any time.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Web Storage accepts only string keys and values. A small object can be written with `JSON.stringify` and read with `JSON.parse`, but parsing alone does not prove that the result has the expected fields or came from the current application version.

A reader should handle a missing key, malformed JSON, an outdated version, and a value changed through developer tools or another script. It should return a safe default instead of preventing the page from starting.

For example, a settings object can include `version: 1` and a theme restricted to `light` or `dark`. Any other structure is ignored and replaced by the default settings.

Writes also need a failure path because `setItem` can throw when storage access is denied or a quota is exceeded. The interface should keep working in memory and tell the user only when losing persistence matters.

Keep the record small and update it infrequently. Large collections, indexes, blobs, transactions, or heavy write traffic are better handled by IndexedDB or a backend.

sections.title: Stored JSON is untrusted input
sections.content: The bytes may have been produced by an older release, manually edited, partially migrated, or copied from an invalid state. Runtime validation turns the parsed JavaScript value into application data. A version field gives migrations an explicit decision point instead of guessing from missing properties.

sections.title: Failure should reduce persistence, not correctness
sections.content: A private browsing policy, disabled storage, sandboxed context, or quota decision can make an otherwise valid write fail. Core state should already exist in memory so the user can continue. Persistence code can return a success flag and the UI can decide whether a warning is useful. Repeated synchronous serialization on every keystroke should be debounced or moved to a more suitable store.

sections.title: Safe read path
sections.content:
getItem(key)
  ├─ null → default
  └─ string → JSON.parse
               ├─ throws → default
               └─ value → validate shape and version
                            ├─ valid → use
                            └─ invalid → default
